final_message:
All five versions build with the provided scripts and pass all three samples (s1, s2, s3), byte for byte with LF line endings. They also match a Python reference implementation on 32 extra random inputs. These cover alphabets of 1–26 letters in shuffled order, costs of 0 and 1000 (including no triangle inequality), and strings from 1 to 3000 letters. On two benchmark-sized inputs (300 pairs, lengths 100–1000), all five give identical totals.

## Algorithm
I used the standard O(n·m) DP, keeping only one or two rows, with three changes for speed:
1. **The shorter string becomes the rows.** The problem is symmetric if you swap insert and delete costs and transpose the substitution table, so the longer string always runs along the inner loop.
2. **Shifted values.** Each row stores `E[j] = D[i][j] − (sum of the first j insertion costs of t)`. The recurrence becomes `E[j] = min(E'[j]+del[s_i], E'[j−1]+Q[s_i][j], E[j−1])`, where `Q[a][j] = sub[a][t_j] − ins[t_j]`. The only step that depends on the previous cell in the same row is now a plain running minimum, so the rest can be vectorised. The result is `E[m]` plus the total insertion cost of t, which is exactly the spec's recurrence.
3. **Lookup tables per pair.** For each letter that occurs in the row string, a `Q` row is built once per pair, so the inner loop reads memory in order with no table lookups.

Values use 32-bit integers when `(n+m+2)·maxCost` is safely within range, and a 64-bit path otherwise. To check the fallback paths, I forced them in temporary builds of each language and they passed all tests.

## Speed choices per language
| Version | Main choices | Time on a 90M-cell input* |
|---|---|---|
| **C++** | AVX2 code (checked at runtime with a scalar fallback): 8 cells per step, running minimum done inside the register (3 shift-and-min steps), carry between blocks costs one `min`. Whole file read at once, hand-written parser, output written in one call. | ~37 ms |
| **C#** | The same AVX2 code via `System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.Avx2`, with unsafe pointers. `TieredCompilation=false` in the csproj so the hot loop is fully optimised from the first call. Most of the time is .NET startup (~90 ms). | ~110 ms |
| **Go** | Scalar code that handles **two rows per pass** (the second row uses the first row's cells as they are produced), which was about 20% faster. Slices are arranged so the bounds checks disappear and `min` compiles to `CMOV`. | ~112 ms |
| **JS** | Two rows per pass on `Int32Array`. Branch-free `min` using `t & (t>>31)` plus `\|0` everywhere: V8 uses branches for `min`, which mispredict on this data, so this was 2–3× faster than `if` or `Math.min`. | ~260 ms |
| **Java** | Two rows per pass in small `sweep2`/`sweep1` methods, so C2 compiles them quickly as normal methods (the JIT warmup was the biggest cost). The Vector API isn't usable because `run.cmd` can't pass the flags it needs. About 190 ms is JVM startup. | ~330 ms |

\*Best of 5 runs, including process startup, on 300 pairs of 100–1000 letters. That is about 90M cells, more than the spec's ~60M. Other programs were running on the machine, so timings varied by ±30%.

I left a `tools/` folder with the test scripts (`gen.py`, `ref.py`, `check.sh`, `timeit.py`, `node.sh`), the 32 test inputs with their expected outputs, and the two large benchmark-sized inputs. I deleted the temporary builds.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
